strategy: The solution is a deterministic constraint-repair pipeline that needs no language model.

Deterministic parse, then error-correcting reconstruction; no LLM is used. The parser reads the column order from the COLUMNS line and splits every row line with one tolerant separator regex. It drops lines that are not plausible data, such as page markers, and pools each section's tokens. A cyclic dynamic-programming alignment groups the tokens into CODE/QTY/UNIT/AMOUNT rows, which undoes wrapped and merged rows and skips stray tokens. Codes are fixed by mapping look-alike characters and then searching single edits, falling back to double edits, until the check digit validates. Each numeric field gets a cost-ranked candidate set: substitutions undoing known misreads, removal of a doubled digit, insertion of a lost digit, and a lost decimal mark. Each row keeps the cheapest triples with QTY×UNIT = AMOUNT, plus "wildcard" options for a badly damaged field. Section SUBTOTALs, and then the TOTAL, pick between ambiguous rows or rebuild a row's amount.

Deterministic parse-and-repair in one code node. The node reads the column order and separator from the `COLUMNS` line, groups the remaining lines by section, and splits each row line into one token stream per section, so wrapped and merged rows sort themselves out. Noise lines and stray tokens are dropped by a small dynamic-programming segmentation that scores how well each token fits its column type. Each CODE is repaired by searching for the fewest damage edits (look-alike swaps, the listed digit misreads, lost or doubled digits) that pass the check-digit rule. QTY, UNIT and AMOUNT are fixed together by searching edit variants for the cheapest set where QTY × UNIT = AMOUNT, scored with a damage-aware edit distance. Within each section, the subtotal then decides between near-tied alternatives for a row.

The parser reads the column order from the COLUMNS line, drops stray lines such as "--- page 2 ---", and splits each section's data lines on any separator. Joining a section's tokens into one stream and cutting it into 4-field rows (a small dynamic program that scores each token's type) handles wrapped and merged rows. Codes are fixed on their own using the check digit, trying the smallest repair that passes. For rows where QTY × UNIT ≠ AMOUNT, it builds candidate values for each field by undoing likely damage (look-alike letters, misread digits, lost or doubled digits, lost decimal mark). It also derives the third field from the other two and scores each candidate with a weighted edit distance that models the damage. Each section then picks the row candidates that best match its SUBTOTAL, including amounts implied by the subtotal minus the other rows. Last, the section choices are combined so the subtotals best match TOTAL, within a CPU budget.

The whole program is one deterministic code node; no language model is used. It parses the document by section, splitting rows on the separator named in the COLUMNS line and keeping empty fields. A cyclic dynamic-programming alignment then groups the tokens into CODE/QTY/UNIT/AMOUNT rows, which undoes wrapped and merged rows. For each row it builds ranked (qty, unit, amount) candidates: exact products from single-edit sets, plus rows where one field is derived from the other two and scored by edit distance. Codes are repaired by a cost-ranked search that must pass the check digit. Each section then picks alternatives, by changing one or two rows or rebuilding one row's amount, to best match its subtotal, and a final pass reconciles the sections against the TOTAL.

A single deterministic code node; no language model is used.
1. It parses sections using the document's separator, keeping empty fields, with a tolerant fallback split for odd lines.
2. A cyclic DP alignment groups the tokens into rows. When needed, a per-row bias re-aligns the rows so the total count matches the ITEMS value.
3. Codes are repaired by a multi-level search that weights each damage type by its likelihood and must pass the check digit.
4. Quantity, unit and amount get weighted edit candidates. Row triples come from exact products or from derivations scored by edit distance.
5. Subtotals and then the TOTAL choose between alternatives or rebuild a row's values.

Node 1 parses the sections, aligns tokens into rows with cyclic dynamic programming, and reconciles qty×unit=amount against the subtotals and the TOTAL. It exports verified original/observed digit pairs and the raw code tokens to `state`. Node 2 builds a document-specific noise model from that evidence: per-character rates of misread, duplicated and lost digits. It then decodes each code by maximum posterior over edit hypotheses that satisfy the check digit, summing the probability of every path to the same candidate. If anything fails, the earlier cost-based code is kept.

Next, estimate a per-document noise profile from the reconciled values and convert it into edit costs. When the profile differs from the defaults and time allows, re-run the whole recovery with the document-specific costs. Finally, decode each code by maximum posterior over every 1- and 2-edit explanation that satisfies the check digit, using the learned rates.
change: DIAGNOSIS: Most lost points are in codes and money fields. Damage there often comes from lost or duplicated digits. Nearly all the arithmetic search in node 1 runs on a fixed, generic edit-cost model (misread 1.0, dup 1.0, lost 1.2). That model cannot adapt to a document whose noise is almost all lost/duplicated digits, or almost all misreads, so qty×unit=amount ties and near-ties go the wrong way. The code decoder has the same blind spot. It only looks at two-edit explanations when no single edit satisfies the check digit. A 5-digit code damaged by one lost digit plus one duplicated digit therefore gets "fixed" by a chance one-step misread, even when the document clearly has no misreads. The pipeline becomes a two-pass estimate-then-re-decode graph. Pass 1 recovers the rows as before. A new `learn_costs` node turns its verified original/observed pairs into a document-specific cost table (`state["_K"]`) for misread, duplicated and lost digits, as log-likelihood ratios. A branch then re-runs the full numeric recovery with these costs whenever they differ enough from the defaults and CPU time allows. All edit generators and the alignment distance now take this cost table as a parameter. The final code decoder always sums one-edit and length-targeted two-edit paths, so the posterior over check-digit-valid codes is complete for up to two damages.

strategy: First, parse and align the rows. For each row, list (qty, unit, amount) explanations using one-edit neighbours. When those don't fit, also try every qty from 1 to 500 that divides a plausible amount, scoring qty and unit by edit distance. Then make the sections agree with their subtotals and the TOTAL by changing one or two rows. The one-row change works out qty and unit as a factorisation of the residual the subtotal requires. Next, estimate a noise profile for the document, rerun with costs tuned to it if they differ, and finally decode each code by the most probable explanation that satisfies the check digit.
change: DIAGNOSIS: Each row's numeric repair only looks at candidates within one edit of each observed value. The section search then changes at most two rows, using those same one-edit lists. The search then forced a wrong unit, and even altered another, intact row, to make the subtotal balance. The code ambiguity under the check digit cannot be fixed. The real ceiling here is that the numeric candidate space is too narrow. Candidate generation for rows changes from "neighbours of each observed field" to "exact factorisation of a trusted amount". When a row is not cheaply consistent, every quantity from 1 to 500 that divides a plausible amount is tried. The unit then follows exactly from the amount. Qty and unit are each scored by the edit distance between that value and what was observed, so values several edits away can still be recovered. The single-row repair in the subtotal reconciliation uses the same enumeration on the residual the subtotal or total requires. strategy: PARADIGM: Single-objective noisy-channel MAP decoding. Every recovered value is scored by one additive cost model of the damage process: look-alike letters, the listed digit misreads, lost or doubled digits, a lost decimal mark, and a heavily penalised generic edit. This includes codes, rows, subtotals, the total and the item count, so they are all ranked on the same scale. For each row, candidates come from inverse edits of each field. Values that inverse edits cannot reach are derived from the arithmetic (a=q·u, u=a/q, q=a/u, or any qty from 1 to 500 dividing a candidate amount) and scored against the observed text with a weighted edit-distance DP. Each section is then decoded jointly as "sum of row costs + cost(formatted sum vs observed SUBTOTAL)". The search uses residual hashing: single swaps, pair swaps through a two-sum lookup on amount deltas, and a rebuilt row that absorbs the residual by factorising it. The document level is decoded the same way against TOTAL. Codes are decoded as the cheapest inverse-edit explanation that passes the check digit, and an alignment DP over typed tokens undoes wrapped and merged rows and noise lines.

Deterministic three-node pipeline. Node 1 parses sections and aligns tokens cyclically into rows, which undoes wraps and merges. It resolves qty/unit/amount with ranked candidates reconciled against subtotals and the total, and stores the per-row evidence in state. Node 2 builds a per-document damage profile (rates of misread, lost and duplicated digits) by Viterbi-aligning the reconciled numeric values against their observed strings. Node 3 re-solves every CODE as maximum likelihood over check-digit-valid candidates, scored by a forward probability under that profile. Stage 1 (Y) splits lines by the document's separator, drops noise lines and aligns tokens cyclically into 4-field rows, which undoes wraps and merges. DIAGNOSIS: Most of the lost score comes from CODE fields. Many damaged codes are ambiguous: several check-digit-valid originals explain the observed string equally well, so the code repair often picks the wrong one by tie-breaking. One piece of evidence is thrown away before any stage reasons about it. That is glyph provenance: a look-alike letter in a digit position (O, l, S, B, Z, G), or a look-alike digit in a letter position, means that character was already damaged by the look-alike operation. It is therefore almost certainly the true digit, not also a misread. The pipeline normalises these glyphs to plain digits at once and then treats them as freely misreadable. That widens the candidate sets for codes and numeric values and blurs their likelihood ranking. The tokenisers now return a provenance mask alongside each normalised value, marking positions that were recovered from a look-alike glyph. These positions are "locked". The mask flows through the pipeline to two places:
- **Numeric candidates:** the edit generators for QTY, UNIT, AMOUNT, SUBTOTAL and TOTAL charge an extra penalty for a misread at a locked position.
- **Code repair:** the forward-probability model divides the misread likelihood at locked positions by a strong factor.

strategy: Line-local layout repair followed by a per-row candidate lattice. The COLUMNS line gives the separator and the column order. Junk lines are dropped: any line whose pieces are not value-like tokens is discarded. The remaining fields of each section are flattened into one stream and chunked by 4, which undoes wraps and merges. If the count does not fit, a small type-aware alignment DP takes over. Each field then gets candidates from inverting the damage channel: forced look-alike letter→digit mapping, inverse digit misreads, removal of doubled digits, re-insertion of lost digits, and a lost decimal mark. Each candidate carries a cost. CODE is fixed by the check digit. For QTY/UNIT/AMOUNT the search finds the cheapest triple with QTY×UNIT=AMOUNT. It tries ≤1 edit per field first and widens one field to 2 edits only when needed, under a time budget.

The parser locates the COLUMNS line to learn the column order and separator. It then turns everything between COLUMNS and TOTAL into one token stream that keeps line-membership markers, with SECTION and SUBTOTAL lines as hard sync tokens. A Viterbi-style dynamic program runs over token positions. At each row boundary it can consume a marker, skip a single token (cost 5), skip a whole line (cost 1 if no token parses as any field, otherwise 12), or emit a row. A row is 4 consecutive field tokens that may cross line breaks (wrap cost 0.3), may start mid-line (merge cost 0.3), and may jump over one junk line. Each row is scored by a memoised channel-repair scorer. It builds candidate sets for each field: look-alike fixes, inverse digit misreads, doubled-digit deletions, lost-digit insertions and a lost decimal mark. CODE is constrained by the check digit, and QTY×UNIT=AMOUNT is solved jointly with any one or two fields repaired. The best path is traced back to give the items.

The pipeline is one deterministic code node. It reads the separator and column order from the COLUMNS line, drops junk lines, and joins all wrapped or merged row fragments of each section into one token stream that it cuts into groups of 4. For each row it inverts the damage channel (look-alikes, misreads, lost or doubled digits, lost decimal mark) to get edit-ranked candidates for QTY, UNIT and AMOUNT, and keeps the triples where qty*unit = amount. Badly damaged rows fall back to deriving the third field from the other two, scored by an exact weighted channel edit distance. Codes are fixed independently by a minimum-edit search under the check-digit constraint. Each section then runs a beam search keyed by the running AMOUNT sum, with a deviation cap, and scores every reachable sum against the possibly damaged SUBTOTAL via channel cost, capped so that an unreadable subtotal falls back to the per-row argmax. A second beam over the per-section alternatives reconciles the result with TOTAL, and a time guard limits the expensive derivations.
